<description>
{
 "summary": "Fix a race condition in the scantxoutset RPC by resetting the global scan progress counter before clearing the in-progress flag. This ensures any concurrent caller acquiring the scan reservation observes a progress value of zero and does not throw an exception that permanently locks the RPC.",
 "problem": "Overlapping scantxoutset RPC invocations can race when one scan finishes and another starts. If the new caller acquires the in-progress reservation while the old scan has not yet zeroed the progress counter, the progress sanity check throws an exception before the caller sets up its RAII lock guard, leaving the RPC permanently claiming a scan is in progress until the node restarts.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'Overlapping scantxoutset calls can leave the node reporting \"Scan already in progress\" until restart, even though the scan has finished.'",
  "Commit 5043b75e01: 'Once a scan clears g_scan_in_progress, another caller can acquire the reservation and check g_scan_progress before the old scan resets it. Reset progress first so the new caller sees zero as expected.'",
  "PR description quotes PR #19362 review discussion where Luke Dashjr noted a failed progress check could block all future scans."
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
